name: Abihajil
title: Levite of the Merarite clan and father of Suriel
summary: Abijah (Hebrew: 'my father is strength') was a Levite of the Merarite clan during Israel's wilderness journey. He is known as the father of Zuriel, who was appointed head of the Merarite family group. The Merarites constituted one of the three major Levitical clans and were responsible for the structural components of the tabernacle—boards, bars, pillars, and bases. Abijah's clan camped on the north side of the tabernacle and played a vital role in maintaining Israel's portable sanctuary throughout the wilderness. The name Abijah is borne by several individuals in the Old Testament, testifying to its widespread use in Israelite culture.

keyEvents.title: Suriel appointed as head of the Merarites
keyEvents.description: Abihajil's son Suriel was appointed as head of the Merarite clan during the wilderness journey, as commanded by the Lord to Moses.

keyEvents.title: The campsite and duties of the Merarites at the tabernacle
keyEvents.description: The Merarite clan, led by Suriel son of Abihajil, camped on the north side of the tabernacle. They were responsible for carrying and guarding the tabernacle's frames, crossbars, posts, bases, and all its equipment during Israel's journey through the wilderness.

keyEvents.title: The mustering of the Levites in the wilderness
keyEvents.description: During the census in the wilderness, the Levites, including the Merarite clan to which Abihajil belonged, were mustered by command of the Lord to Moses. All male Levites from one month old and upward were counted.

versions.summary: Abihajil (also spelled Abihail) is a name that appears several times in the Bible and refers to different individuals. The most prominent Abihajil in the Old Testament was the father of Suriel, a leader of the Merarite clan among the Levites during the wilderness wanderings. The name means 'my father is strength' or 'father of might'.
versions.title: Levite and Father in the Tribe of Israel
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Levite and father in the tribe of Israel' is somewhat imprecise. Abihajil was specifically a Levite from the clan of Merari and father to Suriel. 'Father in the tribe of Israel' is misleading – Levi was one of the tribes of Israel, but the phrasing is unclear.; [major] The role 'leader' is imprecise. Abihajil himself was not the leader – it was his son Suriel who served as head of the Merarite clan. Abihajil should have the role 'Levite' and possibly 'father of a Levitical leader'.; [minor] The summary refers to Abihajil as 'father of Suriel, a leader of the Merarite clan'. This is correct, but the summary mixes in information about the name appearing multiple times, which may confuse the reader. The profile should primarily focus on this single Abihajil. A brief mention of others with the same name can be included.; [minor] The last keyEvent ('Other biblical persons named Abihajil') concerns other individuals and strictly speaking does not belong in this person profile. It may still be retained as contextual information, but should be rephrased.; [minor] In the first keyEvent, Abihajil is described as 'son of a Levite', but the text in Num 3:35 identifies Suriel, son of Abihajil, as the leader – not Abihajil as the son of a named Levite. The phrasing is misleading.; [minor] It is correct that Suriel is listed as a child. It could also be useful to note that Abihajil belonged to the clan of Merari, even though there is no direct family field for this.; [minor] 'c. 1500 BC' is a reasonable approximation for the Exodus period, but the exact dating is debated. Some scholars date the Exodus to c. 1446 BC (early dating) or c. 1270 BC (late dating). A broader formulation may be more precise.

footnotes.text: The name Abihajil (Hebrew: אֲבִיחַיִל, 'Avichayil') is composed of 'avi' (my father) and 'chayil' (strength, might, valor). The name can be translated as 'my father is strength' or 'father of might', expressing trust in God's mighty care.

The Merarites were the third major clan among the Levites, alongside the Gershonites and Kohathites. They were responsible for the heavier parts of the tabernacle's construction: planks, crossbars, pillars, and bases. During the wilderness wanderings, they were given oxen and carts for transport (Num 7:8).

According to Num 3:35, the Merarites camped on the north side of the tabernacle. In the ancient Near East, the north direction was often associated with danger and darkness, which may have given the Merarites' placement a symbolic protective function.

The name Abihajil appears at least five times in the Old Testament and refers to different individuals of both sexes—both men and women. This shows that the name was widespread among various Israelite tribes and periods.

The construction parts of the tabernacle for which the Merarites were responsible formed the supporting skeleton of the sanctuary. Archaeological finds of Egyptian field temples from the New Kingdom (c. 1550–1070 BC) show similar detachable sanctuary structures, confirming that portable sanctuaries were common practice in this period.

The rabbinic tradition (Midrash Bamidbar Rabba) elaborates on the Levites' service at the tabernacle and emphasizes that even seemingly simple tasks—such as carrying planks and pillars—were regarded as holy service to God. Each Levitical clan's duty was seen as essential for the functioning of the sanctuary.
